title: The US Just Added 172,000 Jobs in May — Double What Wall Street Expected. A Fed Rate Hike Is Now on the Table.
excerpt: The strongest payroll report in months puts the S&P 500's nine-week winning streak at risk, pushes Treasury yields above 4.5 per cent, and raises the stakes for every NRI holding US assets or sending money home.
body:
The American economy added 172,000 jobs in May, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday — more than double the 85,000 that economists had forecast and the third consecutive month of strong payroll gains. It was the kind of number that, in any other year, would have been unambiguously good news. In 2026, with inflation running above 3.5 per cent and oil near $93 a barrel, it is something more complicated.

The unemployment rate held steady at 4.3 per cent for the third straight month. Average hourly earnings data will be parsed for signs of wage-driven inflation. But the headline number — 172,000 — is the one that matters most for what happens next at the Federal Reserve.

What Drove the Surprise

Leisure and hospitality added 70,000 jobs, more than double April's figure, with early hiring for the FIFA World Cup likely playing a role. Healthcare and social assistance contributed 47,200. Government payrolls rose by 52,000, driven entirely by local-level hiring. Construction added 17,000 and manufacturing added 7,000 — modest but consistent gains.

Crucially, the prior two months were revised sharply upward. March jumped from 185,000 to 214,000 — the largest monthly gain since December 2024. April was revised from 115,000 to 179,000. The total revision of 93,000 additional jobs means the spring hiring picture is significantly stronger than it appeared even a week ago.

Why the Fed Is Now in a Bind

The Federal Reserve has held rates steady throughout the Iran war, maintaining its wait-and-see posture as oil prices surged and inflation crept higher. The strong jobs data removes one of the key arguments for patience — that a weakening labour market would naturally cool price pressures.

Investment strategist Ed Yardeni, writing before the report, had already argued the Fed should "pivot toward tightening monetary policy to avert a renewed wage-price spiral and to cool speculative excess in the stock market." The 172,000 print gives that argument teeth.

Markets are now pricing in a 41.1 per cent chance that the Fed raises interest rates by a quarter point before year-end, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The two-year Treasury yield, closely tied to the Fed policy outlook, jumped to 4.12 per cent from 4.05 per cent the day before. The 10-year yield pushed above 4.53 per cent.

The Market Reaction Was Immediate

S&P 500 futures dropped 0.6 per cent on the report, putting the index's nine-week winning streak in jeopardy. Nasdaq futures fell 1.2 per cent as the tech selloff from Thursday — driven by Broadcom's 13 per cent post-earnings decline — continued into Friday. Chip stocks including Nvidia, Marvell, AMD, Micron, and Intel all fell between 2 and 6.5 per cent.

Bitcoin dropped to $61,100, its lowest since early February. Gold slipped 1.7 per cent to $4,460 an ounce. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which hit a record close on Thursday, was the relative bright spot, with futures essentially flat as the rotation out of tech and into banks, healthcare, and industrials continued.

Lululemon added to the negative sentiment, sinking 12 per cent after cutting its full-year revenue and profit outlook.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

For Indians abroad, three implications stand out.

The rupee stays under pressure. Higher US rates strengthen the dollar, which keeps the rupee pinned near historic lows around 96 to the dollar. The RBI held its rate steady at 5.25 per cent yesterday, but a Fed hike would widen the interest rate differential further, pulling capital away from Indian assets. Every NRI remitting money home benefits from a strong dollar in the short term, but the longer-term signal — that US monetary policy is tightening while India eases — complicates investment decisions on both sides.

Mortgage rates are not coming down. The 10-year Treasury yield directly influences US mortgage rates. At 4.53 per cent and rising, the prospect of lower borrowing costs that many homebuyers had hoped for is receding. For diaspora families looking to buy in the US, the window of rate relief that seemed to be opening earlier this year may not materialise.

The tech rotation is real. The Dow hit a record while the Nasdaq fell — a rare divergence that reflects money flowing out of AI and semiconductor stocks and into banks, healthcare, and consumer staples. NRI portfolios are heavily skewed toward tech. The Broadcom earnings reaction — a beat on every metric, followed by a 15 per cent stock drop — is a warning that valuation, not performance, is now the binding constraint.

The May jobs report confirms that the US economy is not slowing. For the Fed, that is a problem. For investors, it means the rules of the last three months — buy the dip in tech, trust the rate-cut timeline — may no longer apply.

Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics, May 2026 Employment Situation Summary; Reuters (June 2026); Barron's (June 2026); Investopedia (June 2026); CME FedWatch Tool; IBD (June 2026)
